lines.note: Tsumami, tsumamu gives taking or pinching something with two fingers. The eroded initial T is still visible and is restored; the printed principal part ǒda is retained rather than replaced with a modern inflection.
Dedos completes the two-finger definition. Sakana wo tsumamu is the example of taking food or a relish between the fingers; Vt is part of the italic explanatory apparatus.

runs.text: a Sacana com dous dedos. ¶ Item, Zom-

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the example as taking sakana with two fingers. Sacana is a Japanese term embedded within this Portuguese sentence; Zom- starts the additional figurative meaning on the next row.
Bar completes Zombar: the second sense is mocking somebody. The short continuation belongs to tsumami and does not introduce another entry.
Tsumamikoroshi combines pinching with killing. The gloss begins matar afferrando, killing while grasping, and continues with the two-finger qualification below.

runs.text: do com dous dedos: iſto ſe pode dizer por rõca,

lines.note: The act uses two fingers; the gloss explicitly says this can be spoken as a boast or threat. The scan has a colon after dedos, linking the literal description with the following usage explanation.
The quoted boast means I will kill you with two fingers. Mataruos ei retains the printed future construction and attached object rather than modernizing its orthography.

runs.text: O comer aqui, & ali, como go-

lines.note: Tsumamigui denotes eating little things here and there. The Portuguese likens this to a glutton; go- continues as goloſo on the following line. The medial letter is visibly v in Tçumamigvi; its lexical reading does not justify changing it to u.

runs.text: loſo apanhando algũas couſinhas às eſcondidas.

lines.note: Completes goloſo and describes secretly picking up small bits of food. The diminutive couſinhas belongs to the explanation of nibbling or pilfering food.

Tsumamigui wo suru illustrates carrying out that nibbling or secret eating. The whole Japanese expression is an example sentence, not an embedded term for typeface tagging. The printed example repeats medial gvi, agreeing with the headword rather than the OCR gui.
Tsumane is the root or base of the nail, matching raiz and arreigada da vnha. Abrasion affects the middle of the headword but does not require an added syllable.
Tsumaqiri names a small knife or metal implement for cutting nails. The Portuguese object is deferred to the next physical line.
Vnhas supplies nails as the object of cortar in the preceding line. This single-word continuation completes the tool definition.
Tsumasaki here means the tip of a nail, explicitly ponta da vnha. The gloss determines this local sense rather than a modern association with the toes.
Tsumari, tsumaru introduces being constricted or tightly packed. The Portuguese adjective apertado is divided across the physical row boundary.
Do completes apertado. Hana ga tsumaru gives a blocked nose; the Portuguese begins the corresponding description of the nostrils and continues below.
The nostrils are obstructed, as with catarrh. Cadarram is retained as the historical printed form; the nasal-congestion example extends across three physical rows.
After closing the nose example, kutsu ga tsumaru turns to tight footwear. The Portuguese calça- continues as calçado on the next row.
Do completes calçado. Kotoba ni tsumaru introduces being at a loss for words or pressed by an argument; Fi- starts ficar below.
Ficar concluido cõ palauras describes being confuted or brought to a standstill by words. The visible cl sequence corrects the OCR condluido; ri ni tsumaru begins the next example.
Ru completes tsumaru. The Portuguese gives being convinced or constrained by reason; cate then begins the provisions example continued by fiǒrǒ on the next row.

Cate and fiǒrǒ refer to provisions: cate, fiǒrǒ ni tsumaru means running short of food or supplies. The clear initial t in tçumaru replaces OCR f, and the verb ending is ru. Abrasion leaves a gap in Portuguese ma timẽtos; that usable but uncertain spacing is retained instead of supplying an invisible n in the expected provisions word.
Ki ga tsumaru describes feeling oppressed or stifled. The Portuguese begins estar afrontado, and a- at the right edge continues as abafado on the following row.
Bafado completes abafado do coração, oppression of the heart. Ri ga tsumaru then introduces intestinal obstruction, whose Portuguese explanation follows.
Not being able to fazer camara means being unable to evacuate the bowels. This closes the preceding ri ga tsumaru example, rather than defining the next noun.

runs.text: Paſſo, ou lugar apertado, por onde

lines.note: The noun tsumari is a narrow pass or confined place. Lugar corrects OCR lagar; the following clauses specify difficulty of movement and defensibility.

runs.text: ſe não pode paſſar, ou caminhar liuremente,

lines.note: The narrow place prevents free passage or walking. The paired verbs paſſar and caminhar belong to the same geographical explanation.

runs.text: ou onde pouca gente pode defender a paſſagem

lines.note: The additional military criterion is that few people can defend passage through the narrow place. The object of that defensive action continues below.
Aos inimigos completes the statement that access can be held against enemies. This short physical row remains attached to the narrow-pass definition.

The expression denotes narrow places or passes, repeating the sense of the preceding noun. The first component visibly reads Tçumar, without a secure final i; this anomalous but usable reading is retained rather than importing Tçumari from lexical expectation.
Dos completes apertados, followed by desta maneira. This continuation defines the several narrow places in precisely the manner already described.
Tsumashii describes a person as constrained or sparing, here apertada, ou eſcaſa. The scan supports c in eſcaſa rather than the OCR t; Vt introduces the short Japanese illustration below.
Tsumashii hito is the example of a sparing or constrained person. Hito supplies the noun modified by the adjective in the preceding entry.
Tsumaye means trimming the ends of trees or vines. The word ar- begins Portuguese aruores and must remain divided at this physical boundary.
Uores completes aruores, followed by vines and the generalizing &c. The row is visibly indented as a continuation, so its placement is corrected without changing its stable ID.
Tsumayori is testing an arrow by turning it on the nail. The following line states the practical purpose of this test.

runs.text: bre a vnha, pera ver ſe eſta liſa, ou direita.

lines.note: Bre completes sobre a vnha. Rotating the arrow tests whether it is smooth or straight; the scan supports direita rather than OCR dircita.
Tsumazzuqi, tsumazzuku gives stumbling or tripping. The Portuguese trope- continues into tropeçar on the next physical row.
Çar completes tropeçar. Per met. announces the figurative use: nangui ni tsumazzuku means encountering difficulties, with the verb divided at the row end.
Qu completes tsumazzuku. The Portuguese explains encountering or finding oneself in troubles and dangers, with pe- continued below.
Rigos completes perigos, closing the figurative stumbling example. The brief line remains ordinary running text.

runs.text: O mais alto da fortaleza. Vt,

lines.note: Tsume here is the highest part or inner strongpoint of a fortress. The scan reads O mais alto, correcting the OCR ampersand and mair; Xi- begins the example shiro no tsume.
Rono tçume completes shiro no tsume, the fortress strongpoint. This is the example belonging to the topmost-part sense, not the following nail sense.

The new tsume means nail. Tsume wo kiru gives cutting nails, with Latin l introducing an alternative divided at the row end. The damaged initial of ro- resembles r, so that visible reading is retained provisionally although the action suggests toru.
Ru completes the preceding ro-/ru, likely intended as toru, and the Portuguese translates cutting nails. Tsume wo u- begins the distinct example whose verb utsu is completed on the next row.
Tçu completes utsu; the Portuguese specifies trimming horses hooves. Cortar is recoverable from the printed o, correcting OCR Curtar.
Tsume, tsumuru is tightening, pressing, or packing. The visible gloss is Apertar, ou atochar, correcting the OCR Aperur and anchar; its examples continue at the top of column 2.

Continues the tsume verb from column 1: doori wo motte iitsumuru is pressing or refuting someone through reasoned speech. Motte corrects the OCR muorte, while the printed attached Dǒriuomotte is retained.
The Portuguese completes convincing someone with reasons. Shiro wo tsumuru then shifts to putting a castle under pressure, translated on the following row.

runs.text: Por em aperto a fortaleza, ou combatela.

lines.note: Putting a fortress in difficulty or attacking it completes shiro wo tsumuru. The definition illustrates the military sense of pressing closely.
Cha wo tsumuru gives packing tea. The Portuguese begins putting tea into a container, with that container named on the next physical row.

runs.text: boyão ate cima, ou enchelo de Cha.

lines.note: The boyão is filled to the top or filled with tea. This completes the practical packing sense and retains the printed historical spelling for the jar.

Shujin no mae ni tsumete iru is the expected expression for remaining in attendance before one’s lord. The scan appears to print tçumere iru; the r-like type is retained provisionally instead of silently supplying t. Portuguese Aßistir is complete at the right edge and introduces the continuing-attendance explanation.

runs.text: ſempre diante do ſenhor, ou em ſua caſa pera

lines.note: One remains continually before the lord or in his house. The purpose clause begins with pera and continues below.
The purpose is serving the lord. Tsumeshu then names the people who keep such attendance; the Portuguese relative clause continues with sempre divided after its abbreviated first syllable.
Pre completes the preceding ſẽ- as sempre. Those people continually attend in this manner; the adverb belongs to the retainer definition.

runs.text: Couſa q̃ ſe mete pera apertar como cu

lines.note: The noun tsume means an inserted piece used to tighten something, such as a wedge. Cunha is physically divided after cu, with no supplied terminal hyphen.
Nha completes cunha. Tsume wo koo illustrates inserting a wedge; the scan supports algũa rather than the OCR algũta.
Neira completes maneira: some sort of wedge is inserted to pack or tighten. This completes the action example and its explanation.
A separate tsume entry is glossed concluſam, a conclusion or decisive closing point. The visible cl corrects the OCR Condluſam without modernizing the am ending.

Tsumeai introduces reciprocal contention so as to overcome or conclude against one another. The principal forms ǒ and ǒta remain as printed; the visible infinitive concluir corrects the OCR abbreviation-like spelling.

runs.text: hum a outro, l, chegar perto com as mãos, ou

lines.note: The disputants contend one against the other; the alternative sense is closing to hand-to-hand range. The instrument is completed with Catana below.

runs.text: Catana hum do outro pera pelejar, l, dous exer-

lines.note: The close combat may use hands or swords, and the same verb can apply to two armies. The Portuguese exer- is completed on the following row.
Citos completes exercitos. The final &c generalizes the reciprocal close-combat application beyond the listed fighters and armies.
Tsumeawase describes two forces coming together at close quarters. The scan has u in auaxe, correcting OCR anaxe; the definition continues with who is fighting.

runs.text: de perto dous exercitos, ou muita gente.

lines.note: The combatants are two armies or a large body of people. De perto specifies close engagement, completing the preceding verb definition.
Tsumecaqe means pursuing or closing on someone while putting pressure on them. The principal-part ending is eta, not the OCR ota; the Portuguese phrase continues below.
Em aperto completes the pressure sense. Shiro wo tsumekakete semuru illustrates pressing in and attacking a fortress, with semuru divided after xe-.
Muru completes semuru. The Portuguese explains attacking the fortress with force, followed by an additional manner noun on the next line.
Violencia completes com força, & violencia. This closes the fortress-assault example and is not part of the following cross-reference.
Tsumefiraqi is referred to the entry firaqi, firaku. Vide is the italic cross-reference command, while the cited Japanese form is printed in roman type.

runs.text: Cha metido em boyão aßi em fo-

lines.note: Tsumejia denotes loose tea packed into a jar around other contents. The scan supports boyão aßi, correcting the OCR boyẽão aßr; fo- begins folha.

runs.text: lha pera apertar, & atochar os ſaquinhos de

lines.note: Lha completes folha: the loose leaf tea serves to pack or tighten the little bags. The contents of those bags are given on the next row.
The little bags contain tea and are inside the jar. This completes the distinction between the loose packing tea and the bagged tea.

runs.text: Exercito pera dar em algũa for-

lines.note: Tsumegin is an army positioned to attack a fortress. Portuguese for- is divided from taleza on the following row.

runs.text: taleza, ou exercito que eſtà muito chegado, &

lines.note: Taleza completes fortaleza. The alternative explanation is an army standing very close to the enemy, with the spatial relation continued below.
Fronteiro aos inimigos completes the definition as facing the enemy. The term concerns the position of a military force, not an exercise.
Tsumegoi is asking insistently or importunately. The Portuguese adverb is divided after imper-, preserving its printed historical vowel.
Tunamẽte completes the manner adverb. Tsumegoi ni koo is the illustrative verbal phrase, glossed O meſmo, the same meaning.
Tsumegoroshi is killing somebody secretly or without an opportunity to cry out. The scan supports ſecretamẽ- rather than the OCR ſecreianẽ-; the adverb continues below.

runs.text: te, & ſem o deixar falar palaura.

lines.note: Te completes secretamente, followed by not letting the victim speak a word. This qualifies how the killing is carried out.
Tsumejoo names a besieged fortress. The Portuguese poſ- continues as posta, describing its being placed under pressure.
Ta completes posta em aperto: the fortress is pressed by its enemies. This closes the siege-state definition.
Tsumeri, tsumeru means pinching, matched by beliſcar. The abraded m is recovered from the remaining strokes and the two following repetitions of tsumeru; mi wo tsu- begins the first example.
Meru completes mi wo tsumeru, pinching the body. A second occurrence introduces the figurative or ascetic sense explained on the next row.
Ru completes the repeated tsumeru; its gloss is mortifying or treating oneself harshly. Va- begins the proverb waga mi wo tsumette, continued below.

Waga mi wo tsumette, hito no itasa wo shire tells one to pinch oneself and understand others’ pain. The damaged itaſauo is read in that context; its a is very weak. The paired t-like strokes support historical tçumette rather than OCR tçumetre, though abrasion makes that reading provisional.

runs.text: liſcando, ou fazẽdo doer a voſsa carne, aprẽ-

lines.note: Liſcando completes beliſcando. The Portuguese restates pinching or hurting one’s own flesh so as to learn the pain of others, with aprẽ- continued below.
Dei completes aprendei, followed by how it hurts others. This finishes the ethical comparison made by the Japanese proverb.
Tsumetai means cold; the scan reads fria rather than OCR fita. The further sense concerns intense cold or cold weather, with grã- continued on the next row.

runs.text: de frio, ou eſtar o tempo muito frio.

lines.note: De completes grande. The Portuguese specifies either great cold or very cold weather, extending the preceding adjective beyond cold objects.
Tsumetasa is the abstract noun coldness, directly glossed Frialdade. No paragraph sign is printed before this indented derivative; the OCR sign is removed.
Tsumetoo is the adverbial form, marked Adu. The initial is a damaged T rather than I; the printed caron is retained.

Tsumetsukete introduces the example tsumetsukete suru, doing something diligently or continuously. The final l introduces the alternative continued at the start of the next page as tçuzzuqete; it is present at the right edge and is restored. The matching bottom catchword is kept as furniture.
